Other liver function parameters (alanine transaminase, alkaline phosphatase, lactate dehydrogenase, prothrombin time, international normalized ratio and platelets) did not affect voriconazole exposure, except in four studies [ , , , ]. Sequential organ failure assessment (sofa) score Six studies evaluated the associations between the SOFA score, a surrogate of patient severity, and voriconazole exposure [ , , , , , ] (Table ). The multicenter retrospective study by Bienvenu et al . including 70 ICU patients found that a one-point increase in SOFA score on the day of TDM was associated with a 0.19 mg/L increase in voriconazole concentration in multivariate analyses (p = 0.025) [ ]. However, the multivariate analysis included only sex, age and the use of cytochrome P450 inhibitors. The daily dose of voriconazole, which was also significantly associated with voriconazole concentration in the univariate analysis, was not included in the multivariate analysis because of collinearity. In a study including 132 patients, Ye et al . also found, through multiple linear regression analysis, that an increased SOFA score was associated with an increased C trough (p = 0.027) [ ]. In the study by Li et al . , including 125 ICU patients with TDM, the SOFA score was not associated with a supratherapeutic C trough according to univariate and multivariate logistic regression [ ]. The factors included in the multivariate analysis were not components of the SOFA score. In those two previous studies, the authors did not indicate when the SOFA score was calculated [ , ]. In the pharmacokinetic study by Wang et al . including 408 patients, the SOFA score on the day of TDM was not retained as a covariate of pharmacokinetic parameters in the final model. However, individual components of the SOFA score were included as covariates. The two remaining studies were limited by their small sample sizes ([ , ]. Albumin concentration Thirteen studies, including five pharmacokinetic studies, assessed the impact of albumin concentration on voriconazole exposure [ , , , , – , – ] (Table ). Vanstraelen et al . investigated the impact of hypoalbuminemia on the unbound voriconazole fraction in patients treated with voriconazole (20 samples in 13 patients) and in plasma samples from ICU patients spiked with voriconazole (66 samples from 22 patients) [ ]. Unbound and bound voriconazole fractions were separated via equilibrium dialysis. The median serum albumin concentration was 26.7 [13.8–38.7] mg/L. Voriconazole plasma protein binding (PPB) was significantly correlated with albumin concentration according to univariate analysis and a multiple linear mixed model. Voriconazole PPB decreases by 0.67% (therefore, increasing unbound and pharmacologically active voriconazole concentrations) if the plasma albumin concentration decreases by 1 g/L. The remaining studies investigated the impact of hypoalbuminemia on total voriconazole concentrations. An increased albumin concentration was associated with a decreased C trough in univariate and multivariate analyses in the studies by Li et al . (OR = 1.12, 95% CI [1.02–1.23]) and Ronda et al . (β coefficient = −0.023, 95% CI [−0.046-(−0.001)]) [ , ]. An increased albumin concentration was also associated with a decreased C trough according to univariate but not multivariate logistic regression analysis in the study by Ye et al . [ ]. On the other hand, four studies did not find an association between albumin concentration and voriconazole concentration via univariable linear regression analysis [ , , ] or multivariate analysis [ ]. None of the five pharmacokinetics studies found a correlation between albumin concentration and pharmacokinetic parameters [ , , , , ]. Total body weight and body mass index Twelve studies, including four pharmacokinetic studies, have assessed the effect of total body weight (TBW) on voriconazole exposure [ , , – , , , , , , , ]. Four studies assessed the impact of body mass index (BMI) on voriconazole exposure [ , , , ] (Table ). Increased TBW was associated with increased volume of distribution pharmacokinetic parameters (including peripheral and central compartment volumes and apparent volume of distribution) in two out of four pharmacokinetic studies [ , ]. However, Wang et al . did not found an impact of TBW on pharmacokinetic parameters in a two-compartment model with first-order elimination including multiple covariates, based on 746 voriconazole concentration from 408 patients [ ]. Similarly, Chen et al . failed to find an impact of TBW on pharmacokinetic parameters in their population pharmacokinetic model [ ], although their model was limited to

, , ] (Table ). Increased TBW was associated with increased volume of distribution pharmacokinetic parameters (including peripheral and central compartment volumes and apparent volume of distribution) in two out of four pharmacokinetic studies [ , ]. However, Wang et al . did not found an impact of TBW on pharmacokinetic parameters in a two-compartment model with first-order elimination including multiple covariates, based on 746 voriconazole concentration from 408 patients [ ]. Similarly, Chen et al . failed to find an impact of TBW on pharmacokinetic parameters in their population pharmacokinetic model [ ], although their model was limited to one compartment and included only one covariate. Both studies featured a narrow weight distribution, with a median weight of 65 kg and an interquartile range of 10 kg [ ], and a mean of 60 kg and a standard deviation of 10 kg [ ]. When studies without pharmacokinetic modelling were considered, there was no significant association between TBW and voriconazole exposure in five studies [ , , , , ]; a significant impact was found according to univariate analysis but not multivariate analysis in two studies [ , ]. However, the voriconazole dose calculation was based on TBW in most studies [ , , , , ], which could compensate for the potential effect of body weight on voriconazole exposure. Moreover, in the study by Ruiz et al . , the variable dose/kg was included in the multivariate model [ ]. Four studies evaluated the impact of BMI on voriconazole exposure [ , , , ]. In the study by Hoenigl et al . , which included only 21 ICU patients, patients with C trough < 1.5 mg/L had a significantly lower BMI (p = 0.006) according to univariate analysis but not multivariate analysis [ ]. Patients with a potentially toxic C trough > 5.5 mg/L had a significantly greater BMI (p < 0.001) according to univariate analysis and multivariate logistic regression analysis (OR = 1.14, p = 0.024). The dose calculation was based on weight, and the multivariate model did not include the voriconazole dose. In the study by Ronda et al . including 25 patients, patients received a voriconazole dose on the basis of adjusted body weight in obese patients [ ]. A high BMI was associated with a low C trough normalised per dose and body weight in the univariate analysis but not in the multivariate analysis. The pharmacokinetic model by Wang et al . did not include BMI as a covariate of pharmacokinetic parameters [ ]. The BMI distribution was narrow, with an interquartile range of 5 kg/m 2 . The study by Roberts et al . was limited by its small sample size [ ]. Inflammation: concentrations of C-reactive protein and procalcitonin Ten studies, including four pharmacokinetic studies (Table ), assessed the association between systemic inflammation and the voriconazole C trough in ICU patients[ , , , , , , – , ]. Ruiz et al . reported an association between a CRP concentration > 100 mg/L and supratherapeutic voriconazole concentrations via both univariate and multivariate analyses in a prospective study including 33 patients [ ]. The median CRP concentrations were not provided. In a retrospective study including 50 COVID-19 patients, Gatti et al. reported a significant association between voriconazole concentrations and both CRP and procalcitonin (PCT) concentrations via receiver operating characteristic curve analysis [ ]. In this study, the sensitivities for predicting a voriconazole C trough > 3 mg/L were 52% for CRP values > 115 mg/L and 59% for PCT values > 0.3 ng/mL. Two pharmacokinetic studies, including one conducted exclusively in patients with COVID-19, found a negative association between CRP concentrations and total clearance of the drug, indicating that increased CRP was associated with increased voriconazole concentrations [ , ]. The strength of these studies was reinforced by the inclusion of multiple covariates in the estimation of total clearance. Six other retrospective studies, including two pharmacokinetic studies, did not find any association between CRP (n = 4) or PCT (n = 3) concentrations and voriconazole exposure [ , , , , , ]. However, these studies may be limited by missing data inherent to their retrospective design, with CRP and PCT concentrations absent in over half of the patients in the study by Bienvenu et al . [ ], while the extent of missing data was not reported in other studies . Additionally, the timing of CRP measurements was not specified. Genotype Five studies assessed the impact of the CYP2C19 genotype on voriconazole exposure in ICU patients [ , , , ]. Weigel et al . retrospectively classified 17 patients into poor metabolisers (CYP2C19*2/*2), extensive metabolisers (CYP2C19*1/*1), and ultrarapid metabolisers (CYP2C19*1/17 or *17/*17) [ ]. The first three C trough values were < 1.7 mg/L in 15%, 33% and 77% of

concentrations absent in over half of the patients in the study by Bienvenu et al . [ ], while the extent of missing data was not reported in other studies . Additionally, the timing of CRP measurements was not specified. Genotype Five studies assessed the impact of the CYP2C19 genotype on voriconazole exposure in ICU patients [ , , , ]. Weigel et al . retrospectively classified 17 patients into poor metabolisers (CYP2C19*2/*2), extensive metabolisers (CYP2C19*1/*1), and ultrarapid metabolisers (CYP2C19*1/17 or *17/*17) [ ]. The first three C trough values were < 1.7 mg/L in 15%, 33% and 77% of the patients in the poor, extensive and ultrarapid metaboliser groups, respectively. Tanaka et al . reported values of voriconazole clearance determined by noncompartmental analysis > 0.5 L/h/kg in two extensive metabolisers, whereas voriconazole clearance was < 0.31 L/h/kg in three intermediate metabolisers (CYP2C19*1/*2 or *1/*3). Two pharmacokinetic studies did not find an impact of CYP3A4 genotype on the PK parameters of patients with liver dysfunction [ , ]. The interpretation of the results of these studies is limited by the small sample size [ , ], while liver dysfunction itself may reduce the influence of CYP3A4 on voriconazole metabolism. Similarly, Wang et al . found no impact of CYP2C19 or CYP3A4 genotype on voriconazole exposure in their pharmacokinetic study including 72 patients with COVID-19-associated pulmonary aspergillosis [ ]. The authors attributed this lack of association to the limited number of patients classified as poor metabolizers (n = 4) and ultra-rapid metabolizers (n = 1), and to the presumed greater influence of CRP compared to genotype on voriconazole metabolism. Treatment-related factors RRT Continuous RRT (CRRT): Four studies and one case report, including a total of 164 patients, evaluated the impact of continuous venovenous hemofiltration (CVVH) on the voriconazole C trough [ – , , ]. One study and one case report, including 10 patients, evaluated continuous veno-venous hemodiafiltration (CVVHDF) impact [ , ]. Two studies evaluated both parameters indistinctly [ , ] and in one study, the type of RRT was not specified [ ]. The characteristics of the included studies are described in Table . A dialysis pharmacokinetic model using blood samples collected from the line upstream from the predilution and effluent from the output line to evaluate CRRT clearance (CL CRRT ) in patients receiving CRRT was available in 6 studies, including 42 patients [ – ]. The median [Q1-Q3] voriconazole CL CRRT was 1.29 [1.12–1.40] mL/h, which represented approximately 15% of the total clearance of the drug. The total clearance of the drug ranged between 4 and 20 L/h. The mean area under the concentration–time curve from 0–12 h after intake (AUC 12h ) ranged between 17 and 65 mg.h/L. These results are similar to those reported in healthy volunteers [ ] and non-ICU patients [ ]. In the study by Wang et al . including 379 patients, 122 of whom were receiving CRRT, CRRT was identified as a covariate of drug clearance in the population pharmacokinetic model [ ]. Clearance increased by 1.46-fold in patients receiving CRRT in the final model. When estimating pharmacokinetic parameters grouped by CRRT status, clearance in CRRT patients was approximately 17% higher than in those not receiving CRRT. The difference in the magnitude of the association is attributable to the inclusion of multiple covariates in the final model, including creatinine clearance rate. In another pharmacokinetic study involving 72 patients, including 25 on CRRT, CRRT was also retained as a covariate of drug clearance in a model that included multiple covariates[ ]. Clearance increased by 1.62-fold in patients receiving CRRT in the final model. In two studies using standard regression analyses, including a total of 278 patients of whom one third received RRT, RRT was no associated with voriconazole exposure in either univariate or multivariate analysis [ , ]. One study and one case report including a total of 5 patients evaluated the impact of prolonged intermittent RRT, defined as 8 h on RRT, on voriconazole exposure [ , ] (Table ) . Burkhardt et al . did not estimate CL RRT but reported pharmacokinetic parameters similar to those of healthy volunteers [ ]. A high CL RRT was reported in a case report [ ]. The pharmacokinetic model was based on 5 samplings performed on the same day and during the same RRT episode; CL RRT represented 94% of the total clearance of the drug. Three studies described SBECD (intravenous voriconazole solubilization vehicle) concentrations in a total of 15 ICU patients under RRT over time [ , , ]. The first study revealed an accumulation of SBECD between day 1 and day 5 in all 4 patients under extended daily dialysis [ ]. A second study reported SBECD concentrations > 400 mg/L after day 7 in 3 of 4 patients under intermittent

report [ ]. The pharmacokinetic model was based on 5 samplings performed on the same day and during the same RRT episode; CL RRT represented 94% of the total clearance of the drug. Three studies described SBECD (intravenous voriconazole solubilization vehicle) concentrations in a total of 15 ICU patients under RRT over time [ , , ]. The first study revealed an accumulation of SBECD between day 1 and day 5 in all 4 patients under extended daily dialysis [ ]. A second study reported SBECD concentrations > 400 mg/L after day 7 in 3 of 4 patients under intermittent hemodialysis, with an average frequency of dialysis sessions of 24–48 h [ ]. SBECD concentrations reached 600 mg/L in one patient on day 13. Another study including 10 patients under CVVH did not observe any accumulation of SBECD over time [ ]. SBECD exposure was higher than that reported in previous studies of healthy volunteers, with a mean C max of 687 mg/L vs 458 mg/L, but SBECD clearance was similar to that reported in patients with an estimated creatinine clearance of 50 mL/min. ECMO Five studies and three case reports including a total of 774 patients compared the voriconazole C trough in patients with and without ECMO (n = 307 and n = 467, respectively) [ – , , ] (Table ). Very high variability in the voriconazole C trough in patients undergoing ECMO was reported, but both patients with and without ECMO presented highly variable median C trough values (from < 0.1 to 12.7 mg/L and from 1 to 14 mg/L, respectively). Two studies found no association between voriconazole exposure and ECMO status. The retrospective multicenter study by Van Daele et al . compared voriconazole C trough on and off ECMO in 69 patients, of whom 74% received venovenous ECMO [ ]. Neither the presence of ECMO nor the squared ECMO day (to study the presence of circuit saturation) was significantly associated with voriconazole exposure (considered a categorical or continuous variable) in the univariate or multivariate analysis. The squared day of ECMO was used instead of the day of ECMO, since the relationship between the day of ECMO and voriconazole C trough was expected to follow a squared function with a decrease in voriconazole exposure just after ECMO initiation, and an increase after a few days of ECMO due to saturation of the circuit. Similarly, the pharmacokinetic study by Wang et al ., including 393 patients of whom 108 received ECMO, found no statistical difference in pharmacokinetic parameters estimates between ECMO patients (n = 108) and those without ECMO (n = 285) [ ]. ECMO status was not retained as a covariate in the final model, because of a stronger effect of other covariates. In those two studies, parameters of liver function and inflammation were included in the analysis. Conversely, three other studies reported measurable impacts of ECMO status on voriconazole exposure. The retrospective study by Hinze et al . including 153 patients of which 52 received ECMO (the type was unspecified), ECMO use was associated with higher rate of below target C trough in univariate and multivariate analysis (adjusted OR = 4.6, 95% CI [1.7–12.2]). The multivariate analysis included parameters of liver function only. The retrospective monocenter study by Ye et al . compared the voriconazole C trough in 66 ECMO patients, of which 94% received venovenous ECMO, with that of other patients who had never received ECMO support or with that of the same patients before or after ECMO treatment (n = 66) [ ]. The use of ECMO was associated with subtherapeutic C trough in univariate and multivariate analysis (adjusted OR = 7.8, 95% CI [1.6–35.0]). The multivariate analysis included several covariates but did not incorporate any liver function or inflammation parameter. The author found no statistically significant association between voriconazole C trough and ECMO blood flow rate nor days of ECMO therapy on sampling time. In the study by Ronda et al., ECMO support was also associated with a lower C trough in both univariate and multivariate analyses. The results of this study and others are limited by the small number of patients and the presence of confounding factors. Administration route Eight studies assessed the impact of the voriconazole route of administration on voriconazole exposure in ICU patients, including two pharmacokinetic models and one crossover study published as a congress abstract [ , , , , , , , ] (Table ). In the two-compartment pharmacokinetic model of Wang et al . , the bioavailability (F) of voriconazole estimated at 84%. This study included 408 patients, with 68% receiving voriconazole intravenously, 11% orally, and 21% via a nasogastric tube [ ]. Nonintravenous (including oral and via a feeding tube) administration was associated with a lower C trough in multivariate logistic regression analyses (OR =

the impact of the voriconazole route of administration on voriconazole exposure in ICU patients, including two pharmacokinetic models and one crossover study published as a congress abstract [ , , , , , , , ] (Table ). In the two-compartment pharmacokinetic model of Wang et al . , the bioavailability (F) of voriconazole estimated at 84%. This study included 408 patients, with 68% receiving voriconazole intravenously, 11% orally, and 21% via a nasogastric tube [ ]. Nonintravenous (including oral and via a feeding tube) administration was associated with a lower C trough in multivariate logistic regression analyses (OR = 4.8, 95% CI [1.6–14.4]) in the study by Li et al . including 125 patients [ ]. Wang et al . also described significantly different C trough values between intravenous and oral therapy (4.1 ± 3.1 mg/L and 2.7 ± 1.8 mg/L, p < 0.05) in their study including 363 ICU patients [ ]. A multivariate analysis was not performed. In the study by Hinze et al . , a significant difference in voriconazole C trough (analysed as a three-category variable) was observed in univariate analysis (p = 0.04), also only 5% of the 153 included patients received oral voriconazole. Oral application was not included in the multivariate analysis. In all of these studies, the type of feeding was not described. In contrast, a crossover study by Karoubi et al . did not find any impact of the route of administration on voriconazole exposure. Eight ventilated patients received intravenous voriconazole for 4 days, followed by an enteral dose increased by 1 mg/kg administered via nasogastric tube along with continuous enteral feeding. The AUC/dose ratio were not different between the two routes, and bioavailability was estimated at 106% [ ]. However, the crossover design was not ideal, as it was conducted in unstable ICU patients, which may have introduced confounding factors. Two other studies, including one large study of 70 patients but only 24 receiving oral voriconazole, did not find any association between the voriconazole route of administration and subtherapeutic or potentially toxic C trough [ , ]. However, the study by Hoenigl et al . included only 21 ICU patients out of 61 patients. In the study by Tanaka et al . , powdered and suspended voriconazole adsorption to feeding tubes was evaluated in vitro and was estimated to be negligible; the pharmacokinetics of feeding tube-administered voriconazole determined by noncompartmental pharmacokinetic modelling in 5 patients were similar to those of usual oral administration [ ]. Comedication with a proton pump inhibitor or steroids Eight studies investigated the impact of concomitant PPIs on voriconazole exposure, including five pharmacokinetic studies [ , , , , , , , ]. Eight studies evaluated the concomitant administration of steroids, including three pharmacokinetic studies [ , , , , , , , ] (Table ). In the study by Hoenigl et al . , which included 40 patients with hematological malignancies and 21 ICU patients, a significant association between concomitant PPI use and subtherapeutic C trough was found via univariate and multivariate logistic regression (OR = 5.31, 95% CI [2.00–14.09]) [ ]. The authors justified this surprising result by the wider use of PPIs in ICU patients than in non-ICU patients as a confounding factor. Two larger studies analysing 125 and 132 ICU patients also reported an association between concomitant PPI use and subtherapeutic C trough in univariate analysis but not in multivariate analysis [ , ]. No associations were found in all five population pharmacokinetic models including a total of 585 patients [ , , , , ]. No impact of concomitant steroid administration on voriconazole exposure was found in six studies including a total of 874 patients [ , , , , , , ]. There was an independent association between concomitant steroid therapy and a low C trough in one other large study including 66 patients [ ]. Discussion This systematic review summarises current available knowledge about patient-related and treatment-related factors associated with voriconazole exposure variability in ICU patients. These data suggest that patients with hepatic dysfunction, high BMI, high SOFA score and severe inflammation are at high risk of overexposure, whereas patients with oral administration, low BMI, and ultrarapid metabolism are at high risk of underexposure (Table , Fig. ). Nonetheless, the overall quality of the included studies was suboptimal, with studies that were mainly single center or retrospective, leading to important biases. Notably, the retrospective design of the included studies results in missing data and a lack of precision concerning the exact timing of C trough measurements. Our findings strengthen the importance of well-conducted prospective studies and support the need for close voriconazole concentration monitoring in subgroups of ICU patients. Notably, the retrospective design of the included studies results in missing data and a lack of precision concerning the exact timing of C trough measurements. Our findings strengthen the importance of well-conducted prospective studies and support the need for close voriconazole concentration monitoring in subgroups of ICU patients. Factors associated with overexposure Settings associated with voriconazole overexposure and an increased risk of side effects in ICU patients include hepatic dysfunction, high BMI, severe illness with high SOFA score, or severe inflammation (Table ). Voriconazole is metabolised by the liver. Unsurprisingly, ICU patients with hepatic dysfunction are at increased risk of having high C trough values and experiencing voriconazole toxicity. Although multiple biological parameters have been associated with voriconazole concentrations, the Child–Pugh score remains a more accurate reflection of overall liver function compared ot individual markers. Importantly, it has been used in both pharmacokinetic and preclinical studies to guide dosing decisions, and should therefore guide dosing adjustements. According to the manufacturer, the FDA and the EMA, the maintenance dose should be reduced to 50% in Child‒Pugh class A and B patients (no guidance is available for Child‒Pugh class C patients). The most robust pharmacokinetic study performed in ICU patients supports a maintenance dose reduction to 100 mg/12h in Child‒Pugh class A and B patients and to 50 mg/12h in Child‒Pugh class C patients [ ]. However, voriconazole may also be the cause of hepatic dysfunction with drug-induced liver injury [ ]. Therefore, some authors recommend the use of alternative antifungal agents in this setting [ ]. Body weight is well correlated with voriconazole exposure in ICU patients, as observed in non-ICU patients, but the impact remains important enough to be observed in ICU patients, who experience dramatic pharmacokinetic changes. According to the manufacturer, the FDA and the EMA, the voriconazole dose should be determined on the basis of a linear relationship with the total body weight (a maintenance dose of 4 mg/kg/12h) when administered intravenously. However, this dose calculation does not seem adequate, as it leads to a risk of overexposure in obese patients while potentially causing underexposure in patients with a low BMI – a risk that has not yet been clearly demonstrated [ ]. The prevalence of obesity is increasing and is approximately 20% in ICU patients, and even higher in some countries; obesity may play a significant role in voriconazole overexposure [ ]. Instead, some authors recommend a dose calculation of the maintenance dose on the basis of ideal body weight or adjusted body weight [ , ], together with TDM. The negative impact of inflammation on cytochrome P450 expression (particularly CYP2C19 and CYP3A4) and voriconazole exposure has been well described during the last decade [ ]. Overexposure is frequently observed in ICU patients experiencing inflammation [ , ]. However, the importance of this relationship has yet to be determined. Dose adaptation cannot be recommended according to the CRP or PCT concentration, especially as the inflammation status may vary significantly within a few days. Close monitoring of voriconazole concentrations is needed in patients with a previous satisfying C trough who develop sepsis or, on the contrary, who are recovering from sepsis. Finally, high SOFA scores are also associated with voriconazole overexposure. Indeed, high SOFA scores are associated with both hepatic dysfunction and intense systemic inflammation, which in turn contribute to the downregulation of cytochrome P450 enzyme expression. Patients with SOFA scores ≥ 7 require close monitoring of voriconazole concentrations. Factors associated with underexposure The following situations are associated with a risk of voriconazole underexposure and, therefore, at risk of treatment failure: oral administration (including administration via a nasogastric tube) and low BMI (Table ). Oral administration is sometimes chosen for ICU patients because of the increased risk of SBECD accumulation in patients with kidney failure. However, several studies have demonstrated underexposure in ICU patients receiving nonintravenous voriconazole. ICU patients receiving voriconazole via nasogastric tube are often simultaneously on enteral nutrition, which may reduce the drug’s absorption. Given the current state of knowledge, dose adaptation cannot be recommended for ICU patients receiving oral voriconazole. Consequently, intravenous administration should be preferred whenever possible, especially the loading dose. Of note, the manufacturer recommend administrating oral vorcionazole to patients with estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) < 50 mL/min to avoid SBECD accumulation [ ]; this systematic review did not adress this specific situation, as eGFR does not appear to be a factor of voriconazole pharmacokinetic variability. However, studies evaluating the accumulation of the intravenous formulation vehicle SBECD in patients under RRT were not conclusive, and no toxicity was observed. When accumulation was observed, SBECD concentrations corresponded to an SBECD dose

recommended for ICU patients receiving oral voriconazole. Consequently, intravenous administration should be preferred whenever possible, especially the loading dose. Of note, the manufacturer recommend administrating oral vorcionazole to patients with estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) < 50 mL/min to avoid SBECD accumulation [ ]; this systematic review did not adress this specific situation, as eGFR does not appear to be a factor of voriconazole pharmacokinetic variability. However, studies evaluating the accumulation of the intravenous formulation vehicle SBECD in patients under RRT were not conclusive, and no toxicity was observed. When accumulation was observed, SBECD concentrations corresponded to an SBECD dose administered per kg that was at least ten times lower than the lowest dose administered per kg that was associated with toxicity in dogs. Accumulation of SBECD in animals has been associated with liver and kidney toxicity as a consequence of vacuolation in rats [ ]. Interestingly, SBECD toxicity has yet to be observed in humans. Given the current stage of knowledge, the risk‒benefit balance may favour intravenous administration in ICU patients undergoing RRT, especially those receiving CVVH. RRT (both hemodiafiltration and hemofiltration) appears to have a small but not clinically significant effect on voriconazole exposure. Based on several yet well-conducted cohort studies and case reports employing dialysis pharmacokinetic modeling, voriconazole clearance by RRT represents approximately 15% of the total clearance of the drug. All the authors except one recommended no dose adjustment in patients with acute renal failure and RRT. The limited effect of RRT is consistent with voriconazole’s non-linear pharmacokinetics and predominant hepatic elimination. Other factors of variability The impact of ECMO status on voriconazole exposure remain unclear. In the eventuality of such an effect, the effect size would probably be small considering the extremely high variability of the voriconazole C trough in ICU patients. Multivariate analysis of four well-conducted retrospective studies evaluating the effect of ECMO on voriconazole C trough have yielded contradictory results, and none of the authors advised a systematic empirical dose adjustment upon ECMO initiation. Moreover, the studies reporting no impact of ECMO on voriconazole exposure conducted more robust analysis by including the key known factors influencing voriconazole variability. Hypoalbuminemia occurs in approximately 40% of ICU patients, but its impact on voriconazole exposure is unclear [ ]. A single study revealed that patients with hypoalbuminemia may present lower C trough values [ ]. On the other hand, patients with hypoalbuminemia display decreased voriconazole protein binding and higher unbound voriconazole concentrations, potentially leading to toxicity [ ]. Thus, hypoalbuminemia may lead to the underestimation of the voriconazole pharmacologically active fraction. The authors recommended adjusting the measured total C trough with albumin concentration and total bilirubin, especially in patients with severe hypoalbuminemia. The impact of concomitant use of PPIs or steroids remains unclear. While steroids are known inducers of CYP3A4 and PPI are known inhibitors of CYP2C19, the effect of these medications on voriconazole exposure has not yet been demonstrated. Of note, the results of the study by Hoenigl et al . contradict those of multiple other studies performed outside the ICU, as well as the expected effects of CYP2C19 inhibitors. Implications of the review findings Five days after treatment initiation, when steady-state is presumed to be reached, a measure of voriconazole C trough is currently recommended for adjusting the dose. The current literature suggests that dose adjustment is necessary in patients with liver failure and extreme BMIs and that repeated dosages in high-risk patients, including patients with high SOFA scores and severe inflammation, should be performed until those factors are resolved (Fig. ). However, these findings should be interpreted with caution due to the high risk of bias in the included studies. Although our review did not report any change in voriconazole exposure in patients undergoing ECMO or RRT, these patients are at high risk of encountering other risk factors and should also be monitored for voriconazole dose adjustment. The magnitude of dose adjustment should be discussed with the pharmacologist/pharmacist, as voriconazole pharmacokinetics are not linear. In the case of difficulties in achieving PK/PD targets, other azole antifungal agents, such as isavuconazole, are promising alternatives and could be considered even if more data regarding their use in the ICU are warranted [ ]. The apparent complexity of the relationship between factors of variability and voriconazole exposure necessitates the use of more complex statistical methods, such as pharmacokinetic modelling, to determine the optimal dose. Our findings support the need for larger well-designed multicenter studies on voriconazole pharmacokinetics in ICU patients. The apparent complexity of the relationship between factors of variability and voriconazole exposure necessitates the use of more complex statistical methods, such as pharmacokinetic modelling, to determine the optimal dose. However, in the present state of knowledge, no pharmacokinetic model has demonstrated high predictive performance meaning that application in a clinical setting should be done cautiously [ ] due to high interindividual and intraindividual pharmacokinetic variability. Combining TDM with a pharmacokinetic model in a model-informed precision dosing framework could be helpful, with machine learning potentially providing additional support [ ]. Optimal exposure may then be promoted through antifungal stewardship programs [ ]. More advanced approaches, such as those discussed above, may ultimately enable voriconazole dose adjustment earlier than day 5, or even a priori , in order to increase the likelihood of achieving the pharmacokinetic target defined at day 5, beyond what is possible with standard TDM. Conclusions There is a need to better handle voriconazole therapy in ICU patients given the high pharmacokinetic variability of voriconazole, the associations between exposure and both efficacy and toxicity, and the poor outcomes in this high mortality rate population. Dose adaptation is required in patients with liver dysfunction and a high BMI, whereas close voriconazole C trough monitoring should be performed in other subgroups of patients displaying risk factors for pharmacokinetic variability. Combining pharmacokinetic modelling and TDM with a model-informed precision dosing framework may help decrease the variability of voriconazole C trough . chunks.content: Introduction Multimorbidity is defined as the presence of multiple chronic health conditions in a single individual [ ]. It is common in the primary care setting [ , ] and has serious implications for both the patient [ – ] and the healthcare system [ , ]. While it is essential to invest resources and develop interventions to address multimorbidity, there remains ambiguity in defining and measuring multimorbidity [ – ]. An earlier review identified multiple definitions of multimorbidity without much convergence [ ]. While the World Health Organisation defines multimorbidity as “ being affected by two or more chronic health conditions ” [ ], and the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality defines multiple chronic conditions as presence of “two or more chronic physical or mental health conditions” [ ], the European General Practice Research Network adopts a more comprehensive approach and defines multimorbidity as “ any combination of chronic disease with at least one other disease (acute or chronic) or bio-psychosocial factor (associated or not) or somatic risk factor ” [ , ]. While the definition by World Health Organisation is limited to chronic conditions, the definition by European General Practice Research Network includes both chronic and acute conditions, along with risk factors and biopsychosocial factors. None of the above recommend a list of conditions to be used in defining multimorbidity, which may result in different prevalence estimates generated across different settings using the same definition. There is no universal framework for adoption locally for defining multimorbidity with several areas of heterogeneity, namely, 1) definition of chronic conditions, 2) the list of conditions considered, 3) the cut-off for the conditions used, and 4) the data sources to confirm conditions. There is reported lack of consistency in defining a chronic condition [ , ], considering it has been defined as a multi-faceted concept [ ]. Two systematic reviews have reported the list of conditions to vary between 5 to 335 [ ], and from 2 to more than 50 [ ], highlighting heterogeneity in the reported list of conditions. Three systematic reviews reported varying cut-offs (2, 3 or 4 or more conditions) used by included studies for defining multimorbidity illustrating the heterogeneity and lack of consensus in adoption of a cut-off for the number of conditions [ , , ]. Data sources to measure multimorbidity were also reported to vary between patient self-reports (55% of studies) or medical records and administrative databases (42% of studies) or a combination of the two (1% of studies) further illustrating the heterogeneity [ ]. Depending on how multimorbidity is measured, the prevalence can range from 13% to 72% in population-based studies and 4% to 99% in primary care-based studies [ ]. This variation is concerning as it impedes the quantification of multimorbidity burden and subsequent practice changes to improve patient outcomes. The existing areas of heterogeneity articulated above hold true for Singapore as well. In fact, within Singapore, one study reported that the prevalence of multimorbidity in primary care varied between 6% to 17% [ ]. It is important to describe multimorbidity within a specified setting as its prevalence has been reported to vary across different settings [ ], with reliability of measures in one setting not translating completely into another setting [ ]. Moreover, previous studies have also adopted such a setting-specific approach [ , ]. We focussed on primary care specific definition of multimorbidity as the commonly seen conditions in primary care (hypertension, depression, anxiety, arthritis etc.) [ ] differ from other care settings like emergency department (injuries, lower respiratory tract infections, poisonings etc.) [ ] or inpatient setting (septicaemia, pneumonia, complications of diabetes etc.) [ , ], necessitating a relatively different list of conditions to measure multimorbidity. With this setting-specific approach, primary care is aptly suited to provide patient-centred holistic care for patients with multiple chronic conditions based on the tenets of continuity, coordination and comprehensiveness [ ]. Almost eight in ten consultations in a primary care setting may involve a patient with multiple chronic conditions [ ]. From a management perspective, primary care setting is aptly suited to manage multimorbidity with the ability to adopt the paradigm of “goal orientation” as opposed to “disease orientation” [ ]. Additionally, it is established that multimorbidity management within primary care setting is more cost-effective as compared to other care settings [ ]. Hence, for the current study, we focussed on developing a consensus-derived definition of multimorbidity within the primary care setting. With current lack of a universally recommended approach to defining multimorbidity, it is important to adapt the existing multimorbidity concepts based on contextual relevance and consensus opinion of experts since “locally-generated research evidence” is more likely to be translated into practice as it is highly valued by the policy makers and practitioners [ ]. Hence, the current study is based within Singapore’s primary care setting, which is also aligned with the intention of translating the research findings from this study into practice changes to improve multimorbidity management. From an implementation perspective, it is essential to engage local stakeholders as the research efforts aimed at improving outcomes of intended end-users at scale have the greatest impact when the knowledge generation and application are shared between researchers and stakeholders [ , ]. This shared responsibility is achieved by co-production of knowledge between researchers and relevant stakeholders [ ]. The potential implication of developing this consensus-derived definition of multimorbidity will be providing a standardised approach to measuring multimorbidity, which will serve as a pre-requisite for planning, resource allocation and programme implementation to improve outcomes of patients with multimorbidity at the national level. This will eventually support development of relevant clinical practice recommendations to help clinicians better manage such patients, ensure continuity of care [ ], improve patient outcomes like quality of life [ ] and prevent adverse outcomes related to polypharmacy [ ]. While local efforts within Singapore to describe multimorbidity are promising [ , , – ], there still remains heterogeneity in both the overall methodology and the list of chronic conditions considered. Thus, we aimed to conduct a Delphi study to gain consensus on the definition, conceptualisation of multimorbidity, and the list of chronic conditions used to measure multimorbidity in Singapore’s primary care setting. Methods Design Consensus designs like the Delphi technique or the Nominal Group Technique are “ group facilitation approaches which aim to determine the level of consensus among a group of experts (stakeholders) by aggregation of opinions into refined agreed opinion ” [ ]. The consensus-based approach was chosen as it allows balanced participation from all group members compared to qualitative approaches like focus group discussions which may be dominated or influenced by individual group members. We specifically used the Delphi technique for consensus building in our study considering the time and geographical challenges of scheduling face-to-face discussions under the Nominal Group Technique [ ]. Additionally, our study was conducted during the COVID-19 pandemic, which further limited mobility and social gathering. Our study was approved by the National University of Singapore’s Institutional Review Board (NUS-IRB-2020-248). Findings are reported in accordance with the Recommendations for the Conducting and REporting of DElphi Studies (CREDES) [ ] (Please refer to ). Consensus criteria For Likert scale rating questions rated from 1 (labelled “of limited importance for making a decision”) to 9 (labelled as “critical for making a decision”), the scores were categorised into the following three categories: 1–3 (limited importance), 4–6 (important but not critical) and 7–9 (critical) [ ]. A pre-defined standardised threshold for consensus was applied for quantitative Delphi rounds (2 and above): any item with a rating of 7–9 by 70% or more of the panellists and 1–3 by 15% or fewer panellists was included in the conceptualisation of multimorbidity. Any item with a rating of 1–3 by 70% of the panellists and 7–9 by 15% or fewer panellists was excluded. All other combinations indicated indeterminate or no consensus response and were carried forward to subsequent Delphi rounds till the above consensus criteria were met [ – ]. For categorical questions with responses as yes/no , any item with 70% or more of the panellists responding yes was included in the conceptualisation of multimorbidity. Any item with 70% or more of the panellists responding no was excluded. All other combinations indicated indeterminate or no consensus response and were carried forward to subsequent Delphi rounds till the above consensus criteria were met. For a question with different sub-components requiring yes/no responses, if consensus was reached on 80% of the sub-components (e.g., 5 out of 6 sub-components), then consensus at the question level was achieved. If not, the sub-components without consensus were carried forward to the subsequent Delphi round. Expert panel members For the current study, an expert in multimorbidity was defined as a family physician practising family medicine in the ambulatory primary care setting in Singapore who regularly encountered patients with multiple chronic conditions in either public or private settings. Additionally, a person was considered an expert in multimorbidity if they were recognised as an expert by their peers (e.g., recommended as those with relevant expertise to contribute towards the Delphi panel). Participants were excluded if (1) they practised in non-ambulatory primary care setting like community hospitals in full or partial capacity or (2) were unable to commit for the entire Delphi process. Since the recommended sample size for Delphi panels ranges between 10 to 50 [ ], we aimed to recruit a total of 50 panellists. Factoring in a response rate of about 70%, we sought 70 nominations. Recruitment of expert panel members Adopting purposive sampling and leveraging on the study team’s contacts, we engaged key personnel in each of the following five institutions/organisations: 1) National Healthcare Group Polyclinics, 2) National University Polyclinics, 3) SingHealth Polyclinics, 4) Singapore Medical Association and 5) College of Family Physicians, Singapore. These key personnel nominated family physicians who met the eligibility criteria. The selection of these institutions/organisations as recruitment sources was based on getting a comprehensive representation of family medicine practitioners from both public and private primary care settings within Singapore. Potential panellists were invited to participate in the Delphi study via email, describing the purpose of the study and related details. Additionally, they were informed that agreeing to participate and clicking on the link to the online survey in the invite email would be taken as them giving consent (i.e., they understood the study details and were willing to participate). Delphi rounds Our Delphi study comprised of three online rounds with round 1 being qualitative enquiry in nature and subsequent two rounds being quantitative enquiry in nature. The core features of anonymity, iteration and controlled feedback, statistical group response and expert input were observed. The SurveyMonkey platform was used for implementing online surveys [ ]. Surveys for each round were pilot tested to assess the relevance and readability of questions and the time taken to complete. Necessary amendments were made to the survey before sending it to the panellists. To ensure a high response rate for each Delphi round, research staff sent regular reminders (up to two) to the panellists after the invitation email before labelling them as “no response”. These panellists were excluded from subsequent Delphi rounds. Additionally, we adopted a ‘ pseudo-anonymity ’ based approach whereby respondents were known to only one research team member who coordinated the email invites and reminders, but their judgements and opinions remained strictly anonymous to the rest of the research team and the Delphi panellists [ ]. Each Delphi cycle (including survey implementation and analysis of responses) lasted for about four to six weeks. After each round, the panellists were provided a summary of the findings of that round along with their individual responses to inform their participation in the subsequent Delphi round. Round 1 focussed on idea generation and identification of salient features via asking open-ended questions on describing multimorbidity and gathering views on the preliminary list of chronic conditions (for defining multimorbidity) developed by the research team [ , ]. (Please refer to ) This preliminary list of chronic conditions used as a starting point in the current study was conceptualized based on the originally proposed list of 20 chronic conditions by Fortin and colleagues [ ]. This list of 20 conditions was derived from a scoping review of 44 publications with a total of 131 short-listed conditions. The short-listed conditions comprised of a diverse combination of diseases (e.g., myocardial infarction), risk factors (e.g., hypertension), symptoms (e.g., faints) and categories of conditions (e.g., respiratory problems). The proposed list of 20 conditions was derived from the 131 short-listed conditions based on the following selection criteria: relevance in primary care setting, impact on the patient, frequency of reporting of conditions in existing studies and prevalence in primary care patients. The grouping together of certain conditions like angina, myocardial infarction, atrial fibrillation etc. under the category of ‘cardiovascular disease’ was based on such conditions affecting the same body system. The detailed methodology is described elsewhere [ ]. The list proposed by Fortin et al. [ ] was modified to make it suitable for use in primary care setting in Singapore. The grouping together of certain conditions like angina, myocardial infarction, atrial fibrillation etc. under the category of ‘cardiovascular disease’ was based on such conditions affecting the same body system. The detailed methodology is described elsewhere [ ]. The list proposed by Fortin et al. [ ] was modified to make it suitable for use in primary care setting in Singapore. To elaborate, the authors suggested a modified list of conditions for measuring multimorbidity on the basis of relevance in primary care in Singapore, conditions with high burden and number of chronic conditions in a list. The relevance in primary care setting of Singapore was determined by “ consensus reached after iterative discussions between clinicians , research team members and reference to statistics from the MOH and local primary care initiatives ” [ ]. A condition was considered to have high burden if the standardised prevalence ratio was 1% and above in the primary care setting in Singapore. The authors considered lists comprising of 12 conditions or more as per the previously recommended appropriate threshold [ ]. Additionally, ‘pre-diabetes’ and ‘physical disability’ were added to the list to increase the comprehensiveness. Pre-diabetes was added to align with the local context as the Singapore government has placed significant emphasis on management of individuals with diabetes and pre-diabetes [ ]. Additionally, pre-diabetes is part of the Chronic Disease Management Program (CDMP) in Singapore, which was introduced in Singapore in 2006 to provide guidance on management of commonly occurring chronic conditions in primary care and reducing out-of-pocket payment for such conditions by introducing financial measures [ ]. Physical disability was included as it comprised of conditions like hearing loss which are relevant in the Singapore context due to aging population as well as considering the multi-dimensional impact of such conditions on the patients [ ]. While this modified list of conditions was a good starting point for seeking feedback from the Delphi panellists, it is important to note that it could not be directly adopted for measuring multimorbidity since it was recommended based on relative performance in comparison with the other locally used definitions of multimorbidity in Singapore. Secondly, the validity of these definitions could not be assessed completely in the absence of sufficient methodological details. Thirdly, contextual relevance and acceptance by local stakeholders were not known [ ]. Lastly, Singapore has a hybrid healthcare system comprising of both public and private providers [ ]. Within the public primary care, the primary care clinics are organised into three clusters to better meet the needs of the patients. Since the above study was based in one of these three public primary care clusters with no representation from private providers of primary care, its findings may not be reflective of the whole primary care in Singapore. Hence, there was a need to seek feedback from stakeholders across both public (including all three clusters) and private settings to derive a consensus-based definition of multimorbidity. Throughout the iterative process of deriving the finalised list of conditions for defining multimorbidity, the total conditions included in the list at all times was more than 12, which is the recommended value for preventing underestimation of multimorbidity prevalence [ ]. The data was analysed using content analysis [ ]. Based on findings of round 1, the questionnaire for round 2 was adopted. To familiarise the panellists with multimorbidity literature, we shared a slide deck with background information on multimorbidity with the invitation email for round 2. This was done to ensure we obtained unbiased and new ideas from panellists in round 1. For this quantitative round 2 survey, the panellists were asked to indicate their preference by voting on a Likert scale or indicating yes/no . Data were analysed using descriptive statistics to determine whether consensus was achieved or not according to the pre-determined criteria. Only topics which did not reach voting consensus were taken to round 3, which focussed on the evaluation of responses from round 2 and consensus-building on the pending topics. The gathering of responses by panellists and subsequent analysis in round 3 were similar to that done for round 2 (Please refer to and for round 2 and 3 survey questions). Results The response rates for Delphi rounds 1, 2 and 3 were 61.7%, 86.5% and 93.8% respectively. Please refer to for the study flowchart. Baseline participant characteristics are presented in . Forty-six percent of the panellists were between 31 to 40 years old, 64.9% were male, 51.4% of panellists had Fellowship in Family Medicine [ ] and 73.0% practised in public primary healthcare setting. 1. Delphi round 1 1.1. Definition and conceptualisation of multimorbidity 1 . 1 . 1 . Definition of a chronic condition . The most common elements of the definition of a chronic condition shared by the panellists were whether the condition required long-term management (N = 20), whether the condition was incurable (N = 18) and the duration of the condition (N = 16). Other elements of the definition of a chronic condition reported were impact on the patient (N = 12), persistence or recurrence (N = 8) and associated sequelae, including complications (N = 7) etc. 1 . 1 . 2 . Definition of multimorbidity . About 60% of the panellists reported being aware of a definition of multimorbidity. Most panellists (N = 19) described multimorbidity as the co-occurrence of multiple chronic conditions in a particular individual. Another dimension of multimorbidity definition commonly cited was the cut-off for number of conditions (N = 19); however, the cut-offs provided by panellists varied (e.g., two or more, three or more, more than one etc). Some less commonly reported dimensions of multimorbidity definition included the adoption of a holistic biopsychosocial perspective (N = 4), the inclusion of impact on patient outcomes (N = 5) and the interactive nature of co-existing conditions (N = 5). Only 21% of the panellists agreed that counts of chronic conditions are sufficient to identify patients with multimorbidity. Some of the reasons included ease of defining multimorbidity with counts, sufficient for research etc. The majority felt that counts are not sufficient for identifying patients with multimorbidity as other considerations should be included, such as complex interaction between different conditions, biopsychosocial perspective, impact on the patient, the severity of each condition etc. The most commonly reported cut-off was three conditions and above, which was reported by 13 of the 34 panellists. The second most commonly reported cut-off was two conditions and above (8 out of 34 panellists). Other cut-offs suggested by panellists included five or more conditions (5 out of 34 panellists) and four conditions and above (3 out of 34 panellists). 1 . 1 . 3 . Measuring the burden of multimorbidity . Panellists suggested burden of multimorbidity be measured across multiple perspectives (e.g., patient, provider, health system or a combination of these). Patient perspective measures included objective (e.g., disease progression, complications, pill burden) and subjective indicators (e.g., quality of life, mental health scores, etc.). Some examples of provider perspective measures were consultation duration, patient complexity etc. Health system perspective measures mainly included healthcare utilisation and associated cost indicators. The most common response was that multimorbidity should be measured from all three perspectives (i.e., patient, provider and health system). Panellists suggested different sources of data to measure multimorbidity in the general population, including claims data, Electronic Health Records, healthcare utilisation data, medications, absence days, self-reported data and data on social determinants. 1.2. List of chronic conditions used to define multimorbidity 1 . 2 . 1 . Appropriateness and comprehensiveness of list of conditions . Panellists shared their views on the appropriateness of the list of chronic conditions developed by the research team to identify people with multimorbidity. Only six out of 34 panellists (who responded to this question) agreed that the list was appropriate and comprehensive enough to be used in the primary care setting. Another six panellists provided general comments on the limited scope of the list. Apart from depression and anxiety, other mental health conditions suggested by the panellists included schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, childhood mental health disorders like attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, autism, obsessive-compulsive disorder, etc. to expand the mental health conditions included in the list. Apart from hearing loss and congenital malformations, panellists gave various accounts of other conditions which should be included under physical disability, with the two most common suggestions being vision loss/impairment/blindness and loss of limb. Other physical disabilities suggested were neurological (e.g., paraplegia, hemiplegia, etc), severe joint disorders (e.g., gout with tophi, osteoarthritis with permanent deformity etc), soft tissue-related disorders (e.g., tendonitis), chronic paediatric conditions, cognition-related and so forth. Therefore, the original category of ‘ physical disability ’ was re-categorised into the following two categories based on Delphi round 1 feedback: ‘ functional limitation ’ and ‘ cognitive limitation ’. IBD is rare in the Singapore population [ ], and patients with IBD are generally seen in specialist setting instead of the primary care setting within Singapore. The majority (27 out of 34) of the panellists supported the inclusion of chronic pain in the list of conditions and most of them expressed their views from a patient-centred perspective. In qualitative feedback, the panellists shared that chronic pain contributes to morbidity, impacts patient’s quality of life, affects physical function as well as mental health and limits socio-occupational functioning. Additionally, long standing pain requires the patient to modify his/her lifestyle and may need regular review and long-term treatment. Panellists who did not support the inclusion of chronic pain in the list viewed it as “ a result of multimorbidity and not multimorbidity itself ” or a symptom of chronic conditions already captured in the list or coded in the system separately. A few panellists acknowledged the challenges associated with capturing chronic pain. Along the same line, some panellists shared that though capturing chronic pain is important, it is difficult to obtain a uniform diagnostic definition or codes on the ground. Based on these recommendations from Delphi round 1, the original list was expanded to include 27 conditions, and this was used for further voting in Delphi round 2 and 3 (Please refer to and Appendices ). 2. Discussion With the aim to conduct a Delphi study to gain consensus on the definition, conceptualisation of multimorbidity and the list of chronic conditions used to categorise patients with multimorbidity, we reported the consensus-derived definition as the presence of three or more ‘chronic conditions’ from the finalised list of 23 conditions, where a ‘ chronic condition ’ is determined based on the following four parameters: 1) lasting for six months or more; 2) be recurrent or have a persistent course; 3) impact the patient in one or more of the following dimensions: limitations in activities of daily living or instrumental activities of daily living or physical disability, mortality and psychological impairment; and 4) require long-term follow-up. This recommended definition will potentially serve as a standardised approach to measuring multimorbidity in primary care setting in Singapore, and enable planning, resource allocation and programme implementation to improve patient outcomes. Our recommended definition of a chronic condition includes the previously recommended elements of chronicity, namely, duration, prognosis, pattern and producing consequences impacting individual’s quality of life [ ], with duration being the most important criteria as per the existing literature [ ]. However, the exact duration is not universally established, with three most commonly mentioned intervals being three, six and twelve months [ ]. Our consensus-defined duration of six months or more is aligned with the duration recommended by the World Organisation of Family Doctors and the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare [ ]. Our study found the most commonly recommended cut-off for defining multimorbidity was three or more conditions based on both qualitative and quantitative Delphi round findings. Within the existing literature, authors have commonly used a threshold of either two or three for defining multimorbidity with the higher threshold being associated with lower estimated prevalence [ – ]. Our recommended threshold of three or more was higher than that recommended in the commonly known definitions, e.g., by World Health Organisation [ ], European General Practice Research Network [ ], and Agency for

and the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare [ ]. Our study found the most commonly recommended cut-off for defining multimorbidity was three or more conditions based on both qualitative and quantitative Delphi round findings. Within the existing literature, authors have commonly used a threshold of either two or three for defining multimorbidity with the higher threshold being associated with lower estimated prevalence [ – ]. Our recommended threshold of three or more was higher than that recommended in the commonly known definitions, e.g., by World Health Organisation [ ], European General Practice Research Network [ ], and Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality [ ]. From an epidemiological perspective, the implication of recommending a threshold of three in our setting would potentially result in estimating a lower multimorbidity prevalence. However, from a clinical perspective, adopting a higher threshold will result in a more discriminating definition and will help identify patients with higher care needs in local setting who will benefit from the holistic management [ ]. We recommended a finalised list of 23 conditions which is higher than the 20 conditions recommended by Fortin et al. [ ] Comparison with commonly known definitions, e.g., World Health Organisation [ ], European General Practice Research Network [ ], and Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality [ ] on this parameter is not possible since none of these recommended a list of conditions for defining multimorbidity. In terms of the type of conditions included, few panellists in Delphi round 1 suggested adopting a more holistic biopsychosocial perspective. While this was incorporated in defining a chronic condition, our definition of multimorbidity did not explicitly include the biopsychosocial component. Across the numerous existing definitions, some like the European General Practice Research Network have advocated for a definition inclusive of the biopsychosocial component [ ], while others have suggested that simpler definitions are more acceptable [ ]. Our study findings generally align with the international literature on the types of conditions included in the finalised list with inclusion of commonly reported conditions like hypertension, arthritis, diabetes and cardiac problems [ ]. While our definition of multimorbidity includes chronic health conditions similar to definitions by the World Health Organisation and the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality [ , ], it does not include acute conditions as recommended by the European General Practice Research Network definition of multimorbidity [ ]. This exclusion is apt within the Singaporean context of a developed country, with a rapidly aging population [ ] characterised by transition away from communicable to chronic conditions, which accumulate with increasing age [ ]. Hence, from an epidemiological perspective, exclusion of acute conditions should not significantly impact the multimorbidity prevalence estimates generated in our local setting based on our recommended definition. Moreover, the exclusion of acute conditions was based on consensus voting by the Delphi panellists, in line with including conditions with the largest contribution to the disease burden within Singapore like cardiovascular diseases, cancer, mental disorders etc. [ ]. From a clinical perspective, the acute complaints usually seen in primary care are generally less severe and may not significantly contribute towards the multimorbidity burden [ ]. While there were 23 types of conditions included in the finalised list, three were excluded due to lack of consensus, namely, stomach, colon and skin conditions. Panellists qualitatively shared they perceived both stomach and skin conditions to be benign and not having a significant impact. For colon problems, panellists additionally shared the difficulty in diagnosing, which may result in inaccurate diagnosis and prevalence estimation, and perception of colon problems as more of a lifestyle-related condition. In agreement with our findings, a systematic review from South Asia reported less than half of the studies included stomach or skin conditions and none had colon problems [ ]. Additionally, the standardised prevalence ratios for these conditions in the Singaporean primary care setting were reported to be relatively lower (2.52%, 0.20% and 0.08% for stomach problems, colon problems and skin conditions, respectively) as compared to other chronic conditions [ ]. Although chronic pain was included in the final list, currently there are no standardised, recommended guiding principles for documenting chronic pain in the public primary care coding system in Singapore, which primarily uses ICD-10 coding system. This unavailability of systematic guidance may result in inconsistent coding using ill-defined symptom based codes [ ]. While one previous study reported being unable to map available ICD-10 codes to the category of ‘ chronic musculoskeletal condition causing pain or limitation ’ [ ], only one [ ] out of the remaining studies measuring multimorbidity in Singapore included chronic pain documented via self-reports [ ]. As one of the practical implications of this work, we would be engaging the relevant stakeholders in the primary care sector to derive mutually agreed upon coding principles for chronic pain.

While one previous study reported being unable to map available ICD-10 codes to the category of ‘ chronic musculoskeletal condition causing pain or limitation ’ [ ], only one [ ] out of the remaining studies measuring multimorbidity in Singapore included chronic pain documented via self-reports [ ]. As one of the practical implications of this work, we would be engaging the relevant stakeholders in the primary care sector to derive mutually agreed upon coding principles for chronic pain. From the perspective of multimorbidity frameworks, Willadsen et al. [ ] recommended including three categories of diseases, risk factors and symptoms for describing multimorbidity. While the conditions suggested by our Delphi panellists included these three categories, we did not explicitly categorise the conditions into diseases, risk factors and symptoms. However, comparing our finalised list with the most frequently reported diseases, risk factors and symptoms, our finalised list comprises diseases like diabetes, cardiovascular diseases, stroke etc., risk factors like hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, obesity etc., and symptoms like chronic pain, hearing loss, incontinence etc. While from an epidemiological perspective, including risk factors and symptoms will result in potentially higher multimorbidity prevalence [ ], from a clinical perspective, inclusion of risk factors and symptoms will result in incorporation of patients’ views for more holistic management of patients with multimorbidity. Focussing on local literature, our consensus-based cut-off of three or more conditions for defining multimorbidity was higher than the cut-off of two or more used previously [ , , – , ]. Comparing the total number of conditions included, four [ , , , ] out of the five studies from Singapore had the total number of conditions in their list lower than the 23 conditions included in our finalised list. Moreover, for three of these studies [ , , ], the source of the list was not mentioned, which makes it challenging to assess the validity. When comparing the type of conditions included across these studies, our finalised list of conditions included all conditions from three of the above four studies [ , , , ]. For the study by Quah and colleagues, we included all but one condition of gastrointestinal diseases based on feedback from the Delphi panellists [ ]. From an epidemiological perspective, since looking at individual dimensions for defining multimorbidity may result in varying prevalence findings, it is important to understand that the definition of multimorbidity is multi-dimensional and hence, it is not plausible to exactly know the impact of a recommended definition on prevalence of multimorbidity when compared with others. It is more meaningful to focus on the clinical relevance of such definitions along with understanding the methodological accuracy. From a clinical perspective, adoption of a higher cut-off in our definition is more meaningful since it would result in identification of patients with higher care needs, who would benefit from the holistic management in a primary care setting. It is not feasible to assess the accuracy of the local studies as none of them explained in detail the science behind developing their definition. In contrast, our recommended definition of multimorbidity, including the list of 23 conditions, was a result of consensus-voting by a group of Delphi panellists, who had both expertise in the field of multimorbidity and practical insights into managing patients with multiple chronic conditions in a primary care setting. Therefore, our definition is potentially more suited for defining and measuring multimorbidity within the Singapore primary care setting. In the absence of a universally recommended definition of multimorbidity and lack of consensus, our chosen Delphi methodology is one of the most appropriate methods to gain consensus. Moreover, the conduct and reporting of our Delphi study was done in accordance with CREDES [ ], which illustrates the robustness of our study and the validity of our findings. Throughout the study, we upheld the core tenets of the Delphi process, i.e., maintaining quasi-anonymity, practising iteration and controlled feedback, responses of the group being analysed in a statistical manner and compared with pre-defined consensus thresholds and sharing of results with Delphi panellists after each round. All of the above led to the final recommendation of a consensus-derived, context-based, clinically relevant definition of multimorbidity, which was rooted in sound methodology and well-supported by our study findings [ , ]. While existing literature highlights heterogeneity in prevalence estimates based on the type of data source used [ – ], there is no clear consensus on which data source to use. Hence, our findings related to types of data to use will provide a good starting point in the local context to choose an appropriate data source. final recommendation of a consensus-derived, context-based, clinically relevant definition of multimorbidity, which was rooted in sound methodology and well-supported by our study findings [ , ]. While existing literature highlights heterogeneity in prevalence estimates based on the type of data source used [ – ], there is no clear consensus on which data source to use. Hence, our findings related to types of data to use will provide a good starting point in the local context to choose an appropriate data source. For example, if researchers are studying multimorbidity from patients’ perspective (e.g., impact on multimorbidity on quality of life, self-rated health or treatment burden etc.), they may want to include Patient Self-Reported Outcomes as the data source. Similarly, Electronic Health Records may be the source from provider’s perspective (e.g., association of multimorbidity with consult time). Lastly, Ministry of Health administrative data may be the source from health systems’ perspective (e.g., quantifying the healthcare utilisation associated with multimorbidity). The main strengths of our study were having both public and private primary care representation in the Delphi panel and a good response and retention rate across all Delphi rounds. Additionally, we conformed to the recommended reporting standards as per the CREDES guidelines [ ]. Maintaining quasi-anonymity enabled participants not to be aware of each other’s responses, thus limiting the pressure to conform to convergence which could threaten the study validity [ ]. Collecting multiple rounds of responses ensured concurrent validity. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to gain consensus on this relevant and debated topic of defining and measuring multimorbidity within the ambulatory primary care setting of Singapore. Our study has several limitations. Certain components and chronic conditions did not reach a consensus rating at the end of Delphi round 3. As mentioned above, our finalised list did not include stomach, colon and skin conditions which is similar to other local findings [ , , – , ]. Moreover, the locally reported standardised prevalence for these conditions is relatively lower as compared to other conditions within the finalised list [ ]. Our approach of conducting three Delphi rounds is in accordance with the Delphi methodology recommendations, considering the principle of diminishing returns, potential participant fatigue and steep drop-out rates with more rounds [ , ]. Since our study primarily aimed to gain consensus within Singapore’s primary care setting, the generalisability of our findings would be limited. Within Singapore, the generalisability of our findings may be potentially affected by our sample including mainly male and younger panellists. Another limitation inherent in the Delphi technique is that panellists do not get the opportunity for elaborating their shared views. However, this should have minimal impact on our findings considering consensus was sought on clearly defined scope of work. On the practice front, our findings will inform the conceptualisation of multimorbidity at the national level in Singapore, potentially standardising the measurement of multimorbidity within our ambulatory primary care setting. This would subsequently facilitate planning and resource allocation for patients with multimorbidity in Singapore. Having defined multimorbidity, next we would estimate the national prevalence of multimorbidity using this agreed-upon definition and analysing its impact on healthcare utilisation and costs. Conclusion With the aim to conduct a Delphi study to gain consensus on the definition, conceptualisation of multimorbidity and the list of chronic conditions used to categorise patients with multimorbidity in the ambulatory primary care setting of Singapore, we reported the consensus-derived definition of a chronic condition, multimorbidity, recommended data sources from multiple perspectives and the finalised list of 23 conditions (inclusive of diseases, risk factors and symptoms) for measuring multimorbidity. For a condition to be chronic, it should last for six months or more, be recurrent or persistent, impact patients across multiple domains and require long-term management. The consensus-derived definition of multimorbidity is the presence of three or more chronic conditions from a finalised list of 23 chronic conditions. Our findings will inform multimorbidity conceptualisation at the national level in Singapore, standardise multimorbidity measurement in primary care and facilitate resource allocation. On the research front, we would estimate the national prevalence of multimorbidity using this agreed-upon definition and analyse its impact on healthcare utilisation and costs.
